documents.title: The overlooked cost of constant meetings
documents.text:
A survey of fifteen hundred office workers has quantified a complaint familiar to almost anyone who has held a salaried job: that meetings consume the time required to do the work they are supposed to organize. The average respondent spent nearly twelve hours a week in meetings, and a third of them described at least half of that time as wasted.

More interesting than the totals is the pattern of the waste. The researchers found that the least productive meetings were not the longest but the largest, those with more than eight participants, where most attendees spoke for less than two minutes in the whole session. Smaller meetings with a clear decision to make were rated far more useful, even when they overran.

The survey also reveals a gap in perception. Managers, who organize most meetings, rated them as helpful at nearly twice the rate of their staff. Several of the researchers suggest that this is not a matter of vanity but of position: managers often leave a meeting with a decision, whereas those who attend merely to be informed leave with a list of tasks.

Some firms have responded by introducing meeting-free mornings or by requiring an agenda for any gathering of more than four people. Early evidence is encouraging, though the authors caution that such rules can simply push discussion into email, where it becomes harder to follow.

questions.prompt: What is the main finding of the survey?
choices: Meetings are valued more than solo work
Managers dislike meetings more than staff
Meetings take much time and often waste it
Short meetings are always the least useful
questions.explanation: Workers spent nearly twelve hours weekly and many called it wasted.

questions.prompt: Which meetings were least productive?
choices: The largest, with many participants
The longest ones held in the afternoon
Those held without a manager present
Those scheduled in the largest rooms
questions.explanation: Meetings of more than eight people, where most spoke for under two minutes.

questions.prompt: Why do managers rate meetings more highly?
choices: They are paid extra for attending them
They attend far fewer meetings than staff
They enjoy speaking in front of groups
They often leave with a decision, not tasks
questions.explanation: Managers leave with a decision; others leave with a list of tasks.

questions.prompt: What risk do the authors mention about new rules?
choices: Meetings will become much longer than before
Talk may shift into email that is hard to track
Managers will resign in protest at the rules
Agendas will be ignored by most attendees
questions.explanation: Such rules can push discussion into email, where it is harder to follow.

documents.title: Coordinating a donor visit to the new clinic
documents.text:
To: Clinic Steering Group
From: Beatriz Santoro, Development Office
Subject: Plan for the donor visit on 18 October

Dear colleagues,

I should like to set out the plan for the visit of the Whitfield Trust delegation on 18 October, and to ask for your help with three points that remain unresolved.

The delegation of six, led by the Trust's chair, will arrive at 10 a.m. and will spend two hours at the clinic. I propose that they be shown the pediatric ward first, since the Trust's grant was specifically for that, followed by the new laboratory, and finally a short meeting with Dr. Haddad to discuss the clinic's plans for the second phase. Lunch will be provided in the staff room.

The first unresolved point is the laboratory, which will not be fully commissioned until the following week; I would suggest we present it as nearly complete and be honest about the timetable. The second is parking, since the visitors will arrive in two vehicles and the staff car park is already crowded. The third is whether patients' families on the pediatric ward are willing to speak briefly with the visitors, which I believe would be valuable but which must be wholly voluntary.

I would be grateful for your views by Friday so that I can confirm the program with the Trust.

Warm regards,
Beatriz

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the email?
choices: To invite donors to give a larger sum
To plan a visit and seek input on issues
To report that the laboratory is complete
To cancel the visit of the donor Trust
questions.explanation: She outlines the visit and lists three unresolved points.

questions.prompt: Why will the visitors see the pediatric ward first?
choices: It is the largest ward within the clinic
Dr. Haddad is based on that ward
The laboratory is not ready until later
The Trust's grant was meant for that ward
questions.explanation: The Trust's grant was specifically for the pediatric ward.

questions.prompt: What does Ms. Santoro suggest about the laboratory?
choices: It should be shown honestly as unfinished
It should be hidden from the visitors
It should be finished before the visit
It should be used as the lunch room
questions.explanation: She suggests presenting it as nearly complete and being honest about the timetable.

questions.prompt: What condition does she attach to the families' involvement?
choices: They must be paid for their time
They must have donated to the clinic
They must be free to refuse
They must speak with Dr. Haddad
questions.explanation: It must be wholly voluntary.

documents.title: Notice: introduction of a visitor registration system
documents.text:
FERNLEIGH BUSINESS PARK — NOTICE TO TENANTS

From Monday 6 January, all visitors to the park will be required to register at the main gatehouse and to wear a visitor badge for the duration of their stay.

The measure has been requested by several tenants, whose concerns about security increased after two incidents last year in which unauthorized persons gained access to office buildings. The new system will record each visitor's name, the company visited and the time of arrival and departure. Data will be stored for ninety days and used only for security and safety purposes, such as locating people in the event of a fire.

Tenants may reduce the delay by sending the names of expected visitors to the gatehouse by email before 9 a.m. on the day in question; pre-registered visitors will need only to show identification and collect their badge. Regular contractors, such as cleaners and couriers, will be issued with passes valid for six months upon application to the park manager.

We recognize that this will add a short delay at the gate and ask for tenants' patience during the first weeks. The system will be reviewed in March, and tenants are invited to send comments to the park office by 28 February.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the notice?
choices: To report a recent security incident
To advertise office space in the park
To change the park's opening hours
To announce that visitors must register
questions.explanation: The notice introduces visitor registration and badges.

questions.prompt: How long will visitor data be kept?
choices: For six months after each visit
For ninety days after each visit
For one year after each visit
Until the review held in March
questions.explanation: Data will be stored for ninety days.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about pre-registered visitors?
choices: They are not required to wear any badge
They must pay a fee at the gatehouse
They should get through the gate faster
They will not need to show identification
questions.explanation: Pre-registered visitors need only to show identification and collect a badge.

questions.prompt: What is true about contractors?
choices: They can apply for six-month passes
They are banned from the park at night
They must hold a pass for each building
They are charged a fee for each badge
questions.explanation: Regular contractors can obtain passes valid for six months.

documents.title: Head of Partnerships, Tidewell Foundation
documents.text:
The Tidewell Foundation, a charity that funds coastal conservation projects in eleven countries, is seeking a Head of Partnerships to lead our relationships with corporate donors, governments and local community organizations.

The post is new, created in response to a decision by the trustees to broaden our funding base, which until now has depended heavily on two long-standing donors. You will develop a strategy for attracting new partners, negotiate agreements and ensure that each partnership delivers what was promised to both sides. You will report to the Executive Director and manage a team of four.

We are looking for someone with at least ten years of experience in fundraising or business development, preferably within the non-profit sector, and a record of securing multi-year agreements of significant value. The successful candidate will be an excellent listener as well as a persuasive speaker, since many of our partners are small organizations whose priorities may differ greatly from those of corporate sponsors. Fluency in Spanish or French is a strong advantage.

The role is based at our office in Plymouth and requires about three weeks of international travel per year. We offer a salary commensurate with experience, together with generous holidays and a pension scheme. To apply, please send a letter that describes a partnership you built and what made it last, together with your CV, by 14 September.

questions.prompt: Why was the post created?
choices: To cut reliance on a few major donors
To replace the current Executive Director
To open a new office in southern Spain
To manage the foundation's pension scheme
questions.explanation: The trustees wanted to broaden the funding base from two long-standing donors.

questions.prompt: What quality is stressed besides persuasion?
choices: Knowledge of marine biology and ecology
A willingness to relocate every few years
Skill in listening to different partners
Experience of running a very large charity
questions.explanation: Many partners are small organizations whose priorities differ from corporate sponsors.

questions.prompt: What does the application letter require?
choices: A plan to raise a million dollars
An account of a partnership that lasted
A list of conservation projects abroad
A reference from one of the trustees
questions.explanation: Applicants describe a partnership they built and what made it last.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the job is NOT true?
choices: It reports directly to the Executive Director
It manages a team of four colleagues
It is based at the Plymouth office
It needs living abroad for most of the year
questions.explanation: The role requires about three weeks of international travel per year.

documents.title: Chat between two colleagues planning a product launch
documents.text:
Katarina Novak [15:20]: Have you seen the latest test results? The prototype battery lasts eleven hours, not the fourteen we advertised in the draft brochure.

Dmitri Volkov [15:23]: I saw. That's a serious gap. Marketing wants to print the brochures on Monday.

Katarina Novak [15:25]: Then we have to change the figure. We can't claim fourteen hours when our own tests show eleven.

Dmitri Volkov [15:27]: Agreed in principle. But the test was done with the screen at maximum brightness. At normal settings, the engineers say it reaches thirteen.

Katarina Novak [15:30]: Then the brochure should say "up to thirteen hours with typical use", with a note describing the conditions. That is honest and still attractive.

Dmitri Volkov [15:32]: Marketing will grumble, since fourteen sounds better. But I'd rather argue with them now than with customers or regulators later.

Katarina Novak [15:34]: Exactly. Can you ask the engineers to confirm the thirteen-hour figure in writing before Monday morning?

Dmitri Volkov [15:35]: I'll do it today. If they can't confirm, we use eleven.

Katarina Novak [15:36]: Fine.

questions.prompt: What problem do the colleagues discuss?
choices: A battery has failed a safety inspection
A brochure was printed with serious errors
An advertised claim is not backed by tests
Marketing has refused to print the brochure
questions.explanation: The advertised fourteen hours exceeds the test result.

questions.prompt: Why might the true figure be higher than eleven hours?
choices: The test used maximum screen brightness
The battery was brand new when tested
The prototype was recharged halfway through
The engineers had rounded the figure upward
questions.explanation: At normal settings the engineers say it reaches thirteen.

questions.prompt: Why does Mr. Volkov prefer to argue with marketing now?
choices: Marketing has already approved the figure
The engineers will be on holiday soon
The brochure was printed last week already
A false claim could bring bigger trouble
questions.explanation: He would rather argue now than with customers or regulators later.

questions.prompt: What will happen if the engineers cannot confirm thirteen hours?
choices: The launch will be postponed for a month
The brochure will use the tested figure
The brochure will say fourteen hours anyway
The test will be repeated at full brightness
questions.explanation: 'If they can't confirm, we use eleven.'

documents.title: Letter of complaint to a restaurant
documents.text:
Dear Mr. Castellano,

I am writing to describe an evening at your restaurant on 22 March, which I had expected to be the highlight of my parents' anniversary and which instead became a source of considerable embarrassment.

We had booked for eight o'clock, a table for six, and were seated at half past eight. During the wait, no one offered us a drink or an explanation. The food, when it came, was good, I must acknowledge, and the chef deserves credit for the lamb. But the main courses arrived at three different times, so that my father had finished before my mother began, and a dish that I ordered without nuts, owing to my brother's allergy, was served with a nut sauce. Fortunately, we noticed before anyone had tasted it.

When I raised the matter with the manager, I was told that the restaurant had been "unusually busy", a response that did not address the danger. I do not write to demand compensation, though the bill was not small, but to ask that you review your procedures for allergies, which in my view are seriously deficient.

I should be grateful to receive your reply.

Yours sincerely,
Gwendolyn Pryce

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the letter?
choices: To thank the chef for a very fine meal
To report poor service and a safety lapse
To ask for a full refund of the bill
To reserve a table for a future date
questions.explanation: She describes delays, mistimed dishes and an allergy error.

questions.prompt: What was the most serious problem?
choices: A long wait before being given a table
A lack of drinks while waiting to sit
Main courses arriving at separate times
A nut-free dish served with a nut sauce
questions.explanation: A nut-free dish was served with a nut sauce.

questions.prompt: What does the writer say about the food?
choices: Some of it was worthy of praise
It was uniformly poor from start to finish
It was far too expensive for its quality
It was served cold to the whole table
questions.explanation: She acknowledges that the food was good and the lamb deserves credit.

questions.prompt: What does she want from the restaurant?
choices: A payment of compensation for the evening
A new table for her parents next time
A review of its allergy procedures
The dismissal of the restaurant's manager
questions.explanation: She does not demand compensation but asks that procedures for allergies be reviewed.

documents.title: A thriller that forgets its own plot
documents.text:
Few debut novels have received as much advance publicity as Night Ferry, and few have been as unevenly rewarded. Its opening chapters, in which a translator on an overnight crossing overhears a conversation that she was never meant to understand, are as tense as anything published this year. The prose is spare, the details precise, and the reader, like the heroine, feels exposed.

The trouble begins halfway through, when the author seems to lose interest in the central mystery and introduces a second plot, involving a smuggling ring in the port, that has little connection with the first. Characters who were carefully drawn become interchangeable, and the heroine, so shrewd at the start, begins to make decisions that nothing in her earlier behavior explains.

By the closing chapters, the book has stopped asking questions and begun to supply answers at an increasing rate, many of which contradict one another. It is difficult to resist the suspicion that the author had a splendid beginning but no clear idea of how to end.

None of this makes the book worthless. The first hundred pages alone justify the price, and I look forward to the author's next work. But a reader should be prepared to be thrilled in the beginning, and merely patient thereafter.

questions.prompt: What is the reviewer's overall judgment?
choices: A consistently clever and tight thriller
A dull book that has a good ending
A collection of stories with no link
A gripping start, then a muddled finish
questions.explanation: The review praises the opening and criticizes the remainder.

questions.prompt: What problem arises halfway through?
choices: The heroine leaves the story for good
A second plot is added with few links
The translator is killed by smugglers
The ferry sinks in a storm at sea
questions.explanation: The author introduces a smuggling plot with little connection to the first.

questions.prompt: What does the reviewer suggest about the heroine?
choices: She is the best-drawn character throughout
She is a poor translator of languages
Her later choices clash with her sharpness
She is replaced by another narrator
questions.explanation: She begins to make decisions that her earlier behavior does not explain.

questions.prompt: What is the reviewer's attitude toward the author?
choices: Hopeful about the author's next work
Convinced that the author lacks talent
Certain that the book will be a hit
Angry about all the advance publicity
questions.explanation: The reviewer looks forward to the author's next work.

documents.title: Why more cities are reopening buried rivers
documents.text:
For more than a century, urban planners treated small rivers as nuisances. Hundreds were channeled into culverts and covered by roads, their courses recorded only on old maps. Today, a number of cities are digging them up again, and the reasons have more to do with flooding than with nostalgia.

The logic is simple. A river forced through a pipe can carry only as much water as the pipe allows, so that a heavy storm causes the pipe to overflow and the street above to flood. An open channel, with banks that can spill harmlessly into adjoining parks, can absorb far more. One city that reopened a river in its center reported that damage claims from flooding in the surrounding district fell by two thirds within five years.

The projects are not simple to carry out. A culverted river often runs beneath buildings, so that restoring it means demolishing or rebuilding them, and the cost per kilometer can be very high. Residents, moreover, are not always enthusiastic: some fear mosquitoes or the loss of parking.

Still, the evidence is accumulating, and several authorities that were initially skeptical have begun to treat the buried river not as a relic but as a piece of infrastructure waiting to be recovered.

questions.prompt: What is the main idea of the article?
choices: Reopening rivers cuts floods, at a cost
Rivers should be covered to prevent floods
Cities are building new rivers in parks
Mosquitoes have been removed from cities
questions.explanation: The article presents flood benefits and the difficulties of restoration.

questions.prompt: Why do covered rivers cause flooding?
choices: Rivers dry up completely in the summer
Roads absorb too much of the rainfall
Pipes carry only a fixed amount of water
Culverts are always built too high
questions.explanation: A river in a pipe can carry only as much as the pipe allows.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about the city that reduced damage claims?
choices: It built far more parking spaces
Its open river helped absorb storm water
It filled its parks with standing water
It had no storms at all in five years
questions.explanation: Open channels with spill banks absorb more water; damage claims fell by two thirds.

questions.prompt: What attitude change does the last paragraph report?
choices: Residents now oppose every river project
Cities now prefer pipes to open rivers
Planners now ignore all the old maps
Skeptics now see rivers as assets
questions.explanation: Several once-skeptical authorities treat the buried river as infrastructure.
